items.title: The Best Kind of Book Adaptation
items.description: The couple seated next to me at the Metropolitan Opera’s latest world premiere did not stay for the second act; perhaps they didn’t appreciate the puppeteered genitalia that unfurled onstage shortly after the curtain rose. I understood their alarm. After watching a dress rehearsal a week earlier, I had texted my boyfriend: “I am shocked by the size of Hans Vollman’s puppet penis.” Vollman is one of the central characters in Lincoln in the Bardo , adapted by the composer Missy Mazzoli and the librettist Royce Vavrek from George Saunders’s Booker Prize–winning 2017 novel of the same name . Like almost everyone else in the tale, Vollman is dead but in profound denial about that fact—in his case, because he can’t reckon with the tragedy of having expired before he could consummate his new marriage. Hence the outsize appendage: a perpetual reminder of Vollman’s unfinished business. It may seem puerile for one of the most prominent opera companies in the world to put such effort into illustrating the undignified source of Vollman’s grief. In fact, although the puppet might make audiences laugh—or leave—it’s a striking symbol of why operatic adaptations of literature can be so exciting. At a moment when film or TV versions of novels often end up, at best, as decent airplane watches, opera, as the excellent Lincoln in the Bardo illustrates, has the potential to create something bolder and more bizarre. Opera’s lingering reputation for being stuffy and elitist has helped obscure a fundamental truth about the medium: It’s weird. Even before modern composers started testing the limits of storytelling, operas tended to be guided by minimal logic; if you’d like to feel exceptionally confused, I suggest reading a synopsis of Richard Wagner ’s Tannhäuser . And the form relies on artifice to function. There is nothing naturalistic about characters conversing in song with the kind of vocal power and dexterity that could make a skeptic believe in God. This means that there is effectively no such thing as a shy opera—at least not one that stands the test of time. Any opera that succeeds must quickly teach audiences to understand that what they’re going to experience won’t obey the laws of many other forms of entertainment—the kinds in which plot developments are reasonably justified, characters don’t share their every thought in repetitive and excruciating detail, and the gates of hell don’t suddenly open in a dining-room floor. [ Read: George Saunders has a new mantra ] This makes opera a natural fit for Lincoln in the Bardo , a not-very-realistic novel that’s written almost entirely in dialogue. Saunders’s book is set the night after the burial of President Abraham Lincoln’s 11-year-old son, Willie, and is narrated by more than 150 voices, most of them belonging to Willie’s new neighbors in Oak Hill Cemetery in Washington, D.C. Some become Willie’s spiritual guides: the Reverend Everly Thomas, the frustrated Vollman, and a young gay man named Roger Bevins III. Others are stranger and more profane. Some souls have suffered greatly, most notably the enslaved people buried outside the cemetery boundaries, and some have inflicted suffering, including an enslaver whose streams of pure bigotry are difficult to read. As Thomas, Vollman, and Bevins urge Willie to leave the bardo—a space between life and the afterlife, as defined in Buddhism, that’s dangerous for children—the living Lincoln wanders among them. His grief, more than anything else, is what keeps Willie from moving on to whatever comes next. I’ve been trying to imagine what a Hollywood adaptation of this astonishing tonal chaos could possibly look like. (One is in the works , a hybrid live-action, stop-motion film in which Tom Hanks will play the president.) In recent years, the often risk-averse studio system has favored, with notable exceptions such as the joyously bizarro Poor Things , literary adaptations that hew to basic genre constraints: status-cast thrillers with blockbuster aspirations such as The Housemaid and Verity ; prestige limited series, à la East of Eden , that seem destined to wither away algorithmically as they roll off the Netflix queue; and, as ever, the endless iterations of 19th-century British novels, including the recent Sense and Sensibility and the dubious, upcoming Ebenezer . There remains room, in that milieu, for real artistry, but perhaps not for a choice as wild and possibly alienating as the Met’s X-rated puppet. Without the freedom to be truly outlandish, could an adaptation really do justice to Bardo ? I can’t envision a version of the novel that waters down its most outré choices but also manages to preserve its magic. An opera adaptation of Bardo must, of course, pare back. Many dozens of well-defined characters bounding across the stage would be exciting, but also impractical. Yet it needn’t water down: A successful opera is big, and also strange. That’s especially true now; opera companies including the Met , recognizing the need to attract younger audiences, have put more emphasis on developing new works that can make the old form seem fresh. That shift has seemed to breed greater comfort with challenging choices. Among the many contemporary operas the Met has premiered in recent years are a new version of the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice narrated by three stones—yes, stones—and a harsh, mind-bending adaptation of Luis Buñuel’s surrealist film The Exterminating Angel . Lincoln in the Bardo —the opera—is hugely entertaining. It’s full of apt little musical jokes; the most spiritually harrowing scene, in which Reverend Thomas recounts his journey to the bardo, is repeatedly interrupted by the ludicrous ditties of a “doodling Pennsylvanian.” But the show also embraces, and enhances, many of the most difficult elements of Saunders’s novel. The creators have made the striking decision, for instance, to have a teenage girl named Elise Traynor, who is trapped in the bardo in a state of grisly eternal torment, be portrayed by a male countertenor. The uncanniness of watching an adult man take the guise of a young girl helps make that girl’s plight more visceral. It is a constant reminder, almost below the level of awareness, that Elise will never reach maturity. She won’t have the chance to discover what kind of adult she might be—deep-voiced or dulcet-toned, rebellious or traditional, effeminate or masculine. [ Read: The art of book-to-film adaptations ] That kind of layered creativity represents opera’s literary capabilities at their best. A great book creates a private emotional landscape inside the reader: a kind of internal set piece that contains the characters, the space they occupy, and the feelings they provoke. When I open the book Lincoln in the Bardo , I also travel to the tiny, three-dimensional model of it that lives somewhere between my mind and my heart. Opera, like film, can’t re-create the personal experience of reading; the characters will never look just as you pictured them. But it can create an accentuating mirror to that experience. In my imagined version of Saunders’s bardo, Elise Traynor now has a voice. Because that voice isn’t quite what I expected, I’ve started to think about the character in new, unsettling, enriching ways. Because of the opera, she’s taken on a bit more of a life of her own. The most haunting refrain in Lincoln in the Bardo belongs to young Willie Lincoln. Unsure of where he is and why, and desperate to be reunited with his parents, he invents a credo for how he will get home: “never if weak, maybe if strong.” The audience knows his case is hopeless, but it’s impossible not to be moved by his innocent courage, or by the sweet, mournful instrumentation that accompanies it. His words also function as something like an ethos for the opera itself: To stand a chance at success, it must do the thing with bravery, no holds barred.

items.title: Kirsten’s Midlife Crisis
items.description: Photographs by Elizabeth Renstrom for The Atlantic In the early 1990s, when I was in elementary school, a fancy catalog would arrive in the mailbox of our 1950s split-level in Philadelphia four times a year, and I’d hurry to my room to pore over its elaborate spreads. Tea caddies, Windsor chairs, writing quills, ice-cream churns. We didn’t have any antiques in our home, but the lure of the past was so strong that sometimes my sisters, five and seven years older than me, crammed onto my bed to dog-ear the pages too. Most of all, we looked forward to checking in with the girls arrayed there, whose stories we knew so well: Samantha, Molly, Kirsten, Felicity, Addy, and, later in the decade, Josefina. They were the American Girl dolls, preadolescents just slightly older than me, and I was enthralled by the pictures of their period dresses, tiny school supplies, and exotic waxed lunch foods. My own doll was the farm girl Kirsten Larson, a Swedish immigrant to 1850s Minnesota. She had come in a burgundy box, with a slim book titled Meet Kirsten tucked in beside her. I promptly begged for the five other Kirsten books; the historical-fiction series followed the same pattern for each doll, ushering her through a year’s worth of life events, tailored to her personality and time and place. I remember playing with Kirsten in the backyard and having her trace out symbols in the dirt, just as she did with her new friend, a Dakota girl called Singing Bird, in the second book, Kirsten Learns a Lesson . To have such a doll was to own a whole world and the narratives within it. In my blue-collar neighborhood, we lucky doll owners felt that our Boomer parents had entrusted us with a valuable possession, and they had. When they were first introduced, in 1986, American Girl dolls cost a shocking $68 (roughly $208 today). Almost every Millennial I know who once spent hours with her American Girl doll has kept it, lovingly, into adulthood. The dolls’ hardscrabble backstories piqued curiosity about the past. Kirsten’s best friend died of cholera on the journey from Sweden; Samantha Parkington, the wealthy “Victorian beauty” living in 1904 Westchester County, New York, was an orphan; Molly McIntire’s doctor father was off serving in World War II England. Each doll confronted challenges in her young life that felt at once intimate and unfamiliar. Add well-made accessories and vivid history to the mix, and girlhood acquired an allure that Barbie seemed to bypass on her way to her plastic Dreamhouse. Yet as American Girl’s 40th anniversary arrives, the brand finds itself in something of a midlife crisis. In 1998, Pleasant Rowland, the former teacher and textbook writer who’d dreamed up the dolls, sold Pleasant Company to an unlikely steward: Mattel, the company behind Barbie and her stilettos. A quarter century later, the heyday of preteen devotion to playmates from bygone eras seems like, well, a bygone era. Mattel’s dire balance sheets for the American Girl line confirm that the magic has faded. Might a surge of celebratory attention to the Pleasant Company past be the secret to renewed relevance? It certainly could not be better timed, with the Millennial faithful now in their childbearing—and toy-buying—years. With Rowland’s spare-no-effort ethos of product creation clearly in mind, Mattel has released The Making of American Girl , a chronicle of Pleasant Company’s origin story that resembles the sumptuous catalogs of my childhood, only far grander in scale. The coffee-table book is a canny paean to the dozen years of Rowland’s leadership. Extolling her “courage and conviction,” it dwells on her commitment to craftsmanship. The scrapbook-style spreads showcase mock-ups of her early brainstorming, the fabrics she insisted on, the dovetailed furniture joints and delicate details on all those teeny accessories that girls craved and parents put on their credit cards. Designed as a nostalgia trip for Millennials, it works. My 9- and 4-year-old daughters showed the book off to their playmates one weekend afternoon, but it was those girls’ 40-something mom who lingered over it with me, comparing notes on the expensive items we had known better than to ask for in childhood, such as the bisque plate and mug for Kirsten, made by the renowned Rowe Pottery Works in Wisconsin. But what about the rest of the story of the doll that had become America’s second-most-popular by the late ’90s? That’s left to Amanda FitzSimons, a journalist who did not have the cooperation of Mattel, or of the now-85-year-old Rowland, for her smart and colorful cultural analysis, An American Girl: How a Billion-Dollar Doll and Its Unlikely Founder Changed Girlhood Forever . That means she’s free, after exploring how the dolls and books became unexpected hits, to describe how the American Girl brand’s identity eventually grew so muddled that it has become barely recognizable. FitzSimons starts with Rowland’s big idea, conceived on a trip to Colonial Williamsburg in the early 1980s and transformed into an elaborate business plan over a weekend at her northern-Wisconsin cabin, where the woodstove and outhouse had her thinking about life in the past. The books, “for girls about girls,” came first—they were “the heart of” the American Girl collection, in Rowland’s words. A boss who looked for tenacity in her employees as well as her dolls, Rowland liked to say that her initials, PTR, stood for “Prepare to Redo”; a researcher at the company devoted a day, for example, to conferring with poultry-science experts to determine the exact hour at which Kirsten’s hens would lay eggs. With that attention to detail, Rowland turned the business into a high-volume, high-value sensation. Over time, Pleasant Company offered ever more accessories, such as carefully constructed craft kits (I had my eye on a wooden loom for weaving a doll sash), stationery, and matching outfits for dolls and their girls. But above all, what Rowland sold was the idea that girlhood was important, in need of preservation. Her American Girl enterprise, FitzSimons argues, was a mission to rescue an endangered phase of life. Girlhood was slipping away. The term tween , which encompasses kids as young as 8, was popularized as a marketing tool in the ’80s and quickly became shorthand for a child who didn’t act like a child. Late-20th-century girls, Rowland worried from the start, “turn on the television set and the world comes down on them hard. It’s sexually explicit, it’s dangerous and violent, it’s angry, complaining, discouraging.” By the mid-’90s, the phenomenon of kids aging out of pastimes earlier was well documented. FitzSimons credits Rowland with an astute insight amid rising calls to shore up girls’ self-confidence: “It wasn’t that girls wanted to be older,” she writes; “it was that they wanted to be understood, feel important.” The dolls’ figures never matured, and the books didn’t include periods or crushes; friends, school, and adventure occupied the girls’ imaginations. Samantha fights back when a local menace puts salt in her birthday ice cream; colonial-era Felicity Merriman befriends the daughter of a Loyalist family despite her father’s Revolutionary politics. In aiming to transport girls to other worlds, Rowland had more than innocent fantasy and vivid Americana in mind. Her goal was to encourage play that felt immersive and incorporated historical adversity . The books included plotlines about children working in factories and the displacement of Native people in the Midwest. Her cast expanded to include a second trio of dolls—Felicity, as well as Josefina Montoya , who lives on a New Mexico rancho in 1824, and Addy Walker , an enslaved girl who escapes to 1864 Philadelphia. Elizabeth Renstrom for The Atlantic Josefina Elizabeth Renstrom for The Atlantic Addy The panels of scholars hired to help vet the dolls’ backgrounds and physical appearance had their socially charged work cut out for them. Lonnie Bunch, later the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, was part of the committee advising on Addy, whose development stirred plenty of debate over her storyline (whether American Girl’s only Black doll should have been born into slavery, for example) and over specifics (which hair texture was appropriate, how cheerful faces should look in book illustrations). People argued about her suitability as a possession for white girls. (Endorsed by Oprah in time for Christmas 1993, Addy was a commercial success that year.) [ Read: American Girls aren’t radical anymore ] The original six American Girls telegraphed a spirit of optimism about the very idea of being a girl. Rowland’s characters were intrepid and resourceful but still gracious; free to be tomboyish while also engaged with feminine traditions, such as Kirsten’s quilting. Breaking down gender stereotypes wasn’t Rowland’s goal, and “feminism was never mentioned in the room,” the creative director of American Girl magazine told FitzSimons. But the “girls can do anything” spirit of third-wave feminism, cresting in the ’90s, was the backdrop of the brand’s rise: empowerment and education in one finely crafted package. As Rowland put it in a letter addressed to parents in an early catalog, “Growing up in America is, has been, and can always be an experience to treasure.” “I don’t care if a girl grew up in Colonial times, Victorian times, in 1950, or today,” Rowland once said. “The emotional experiences of childhood are absolutely true and constant.” Thanks in part to my own exposure to her dolls’ stories, I confess I can’t quite believe that she ever really meant this. The hardships entailed in Kirsten’s months-long sea voyage stunned snack-happy 8-year-old me; I was suddenly aware of the many conveniences and freedoms that I took for granted. Our kinship was strong—we even shared a birthday (June 8)—but our attachment, I felt, was also about imagining how different my days and moods were from hers. When Rowland sold her venture (for $700 million), the business was just expanding into American Girl stores and cafés, an old-fashioned “mecca,” she called it, for mother-daughter doll bonding (and buying). The world’s virtual horizons had barely begun to be mapped, and the looming kids-getting-older-younger landscape was soon Mattel’s problem to worry about. Over the past two decades, according to one study, the average age at which children begin to be interested in “adult-oriented topics such as fashion and technology” has decreased from age 12 to 8. In 1990, little girls were hoping for $50 nightgowns to match the one their doll wore; now they’re pining for $90 Drunk Elephant glycolic serum to slather on their faces before bed. For Mattel at the turn of the millennium, adultified competition arrived in an unnervingly direct and provocative form: Bratz dolls, aimed at young girls. With their pillowy lips, heavy eye makeup, and distorted big-head-small-body proportions, they were mutant Barbies, accelerants for the idea that brasher and sexier were better. By 2006, they accounted for 40 percent of the fashion-doll market. The American Girl heritage was buried as Mattel played catch-up. Except for Addy and Josefina, the original dolls were retired. Catalogs shrank; chic burgundy gave way to hot pink. Proliferating doll lines—Best Friends, Truly Me, WellieWishers—shifted the focus away from the bond between a girl and her doll, as a New Yorker article noted, and onto friendship networks. Instead of intriguing relics from earlier times—a miniature oil lamp or a friendship quilt—the Girl of the Year doll (the run is limited, so buy her fast) had plastic-tchotchke versions of things such as a cellphone and a Stanley-style water bottle. New dolls that were added to the historical American Girl line soon hailed from more recent times; Courtney Moore, who “never met a mixtape she didn’t like,” was from 1986, the year the brand was launched. The accompanying books became perfunctory, a scattershot array of graphics and a story that gestured at history but never dove in. Even as doll prices rose, American Girl revenue cratered, reportedly falling by 61 percent from 2016 to late 2023. In a recent Instagram post, a mom vented about a visit to the books section at an American Girl store: “Excuse me. Where are the boxed sets. Where are the SACRED TEXTS. The Library of Alexandria, again.” Mattel notably hasn’t bothered to reissue the full book series, though the six original dolls have been rereleased for the brand’s anniversary. Instead, targeting its Millennial fan base, the company commissioned a new book in the Samantha series from the best-selling historical novelist Fiona Davis, whose other work for adults features adventurous young women in glamorous and gritty 20th-century New York City. Elizabeth Renstrom for The Atlantic A Modern Era Kirsten doll, now with space buns and an updated dress, and the six original American Girl dolls In Samantha: The Next Chapter , Davis locates her subject in 1920. Now 25, Samantha is down on her luck in New York (her family’s fortune has been stolen) and working as a shopgirl. But she soon finds the thieves and helps the suffragists’ cause, championed by her Aunt Cornelia in the original books. For some readers, Davis’s aim of evoking “sweet nostalgia” and inspiring “wonder at the women you’ve become,” as she has put it, may prove rewarding. Yet her American Girl audience is ambivalent, too. Reared on Rowland’s vision of boldly imaginative girls eager to play their part in an America that was constantly improving, Millennials are also dealing with disenchantment: The country they now inhabit hasn’t delivered on the optimism that powered the world of the dolls and books they loved. Davis’s grown-up Samantha, though a tribute to the brand’s history-infused approach, is likely to disappoint. She is stuffed with generically desirable attributes of womanhood and faces conventional emotional dilemmas: She’s determined to remain independent while looking for love, forward-thinking yet happy with her lot. It’s a formula for tame likability rather than conflicted maturity. Earlier this year, the latest American Girl catalog landed on my doorstep—it was a re-creation of the first catalog cover, which showed a girl curled up with her doll on a chintz-covered window seat, intently reading a book. But inside, after a few pages dedicated to the historical dolls, was a torrent of brand collaborations (with Hill House Home dresses, Disney princesses, Polly Pocket) and a spread welcoming the Modern Era collection—the classic dolls, now offered in shrunken, all-vinyl versions with oversize heads, and dressed up in trendy contemporary outfits. American Girl has a tough needle to thread (the cliché seems apt): make the dolls of good quality, but not too costly; repackage American history, but don’t offend anyone; get Gen Alpha girls interested, but remember that Millennials now hold the credit cards. I’ve deemed my 4-year-old too young for a $175 doll, and my Harry Potter –obsessed 9-year-old considers my vintage Kirsten books too slender to take seriously. But when an old 1995 catalog I’d ordered for research arrived, both pored over it, fascinated by Samantha’s miniature brass lunch pail and Felicity’s coal bed warmer. I explained that the company no longer makes those items; we can get them only for astronomical sums on resale sites. “But this is all so perfect,” my elder daughter said. “It almost makes them come alive.” This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “Kirsten’s Midlife Crisis.”

items.title: AVAS 2026: Accra to drive Africa’s Tokenisation Agenda
items.description: Ghana will host the Africa Virtual Asset Summit (AVAS) on November 2–3, 2026, as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Ghana, convenes regulators, policymakers and industry leaders to advance a trusted, inclusive and innovative virtual asset ecosystem across Africa. The summit, taking place at the Kempinski Hotel Gold Coast City, Accra, will be held under the theme, “Tokenisation: Africa’s Pathway Towards Building a Trusted, Inclusive and Innovative Virtual Asset Ecosystem.” At the heart of the gathering is the proposed Accra Declaration, a shared set of principles and recommendations intended to guide the responsible development of virtual assets and tokenisation across the continent. Tokenisation—the digital representation of assets—offers opportunities to unlock value in gold, real estate, cocoa, bonds and trade receivables, potentially widening access to investment and improving the way assets are owned, transferred and traded. Ghana is already exploring these opportunities through its regulatory sandbox, including applications involving gold and Treasury bills. AVAS 2026 aims to move the conversation beyond possibilities towards practical outcomes, including policy recommendations, stronger dialogue between regulators and market participants, and cross-border partnerships to support responsible innovation. The summit is expected to bring together securities regulators, central banks, finance ministries, financial intelligence units, stock exchanges, banks, asset managers, pension funds, insurers, virtual asset service providers, fintech companies, investors, legal practitioners, academics and development partners. Among the announced keynote speakers are Finance Minister Hon. Dr. Cassiel Ato Baah Forson; Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr. Johnson Pandit Asiama; SEC Director-General Dr. James Klutse Avedzi; Chief of Staff Hon. Julius Debrah; and Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Hon. Samuel Nartey George. The proposed Accra Declaration will be central to the summit’s ambition to establish common ground for responsible tokenisation, encourage cooperation among jurisdictions and support the development of credible virtual asset markets. As African economies explore new ways to mobilise capital and expand financial inclusion, AVAS 2026 will provide a platform for shaping the policies and partnerships needed to realise tokenisation’s potential. The event is presented with the involvement of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Ghana. Registration information is available at www.avas2026.com .

items.title: Faranah : colère des étudiants après le décès tragique de leur camarade
items.description: Un étudiant a tragiquement perdu la vie lors d’un match de football à Faranah, dans la soirée de ce mardi 28 octobre 2026. Ses camarades pointent du doigt l'hôpital régional. ​La victime est Morlaye Clavère Maouomou, étudiant en première année de licence (L1) au département d’économie rurale, filière gestion des entreprises agricoles. ​Selon un communiqué de l’institution : « Le drame est survenu dans la soirée du mardi 27 octobre 2026. Le jeune étudiant se trouvait sur un terrain de sport lorsqu'il a été victime d'une crise cardiaque foudroyante. » ​Suite à ce décès, des tensions ont éclaté aux alentours de l’hôpital régional de Faranah. Plusieurs étudiants ont vivement mis en cause le personnel médical, l'accusant d'avoir tardé à prendre en charge leur camarade, faute du paiement préalable d'une somme de 30 000 GNF. ​« Quand il a fait la crise, nous l'avons transporté à l'hôpital. Sur place, ils ont commencé à nous poser des questions d'argent, et notre ami a rendu l'âme pendant ce temps », a témoigné un étudiant présent sur les lieux. ​ ​Contacté par Guineenews, le directeur de l'hôpital regional, Dr Ibrahim Nabé, a déclaré ceci : « Le jeune jouait au football dans le quartier, c’est là où il a eu un arrêt cardiaque. Ses amis l’ont pris pour l’emmener à l’hôpital. Malheureusement, nous avons reçu un dépôt de corps, c’est-à-dire qu’il n’est pas arrivé vivant dans notre structure. » ​Au sein du campus de l'ISAV, règnent tristesse et consternation à la suite de cette disparition brutale.

items.title: Constitutional reform must deliver institutions that serve Ghanaians
items.description: A judge may be independent on paper and still struggle to deliver justice because a court lacks staff, reliable computers or funds to operate. A public institution may have impressive legal powers yet depend on political goodwill for appointments and resources. These contradictions should be central to Ghana’s constitutional reform debate. The question is practical: how do we build institutions that serve citizens fairly, whichever party governs? The judiciary provides a useful example. Courts interpret laws, settle disputes and check abuses of executive and legislative power. Their effectiveness affects everyone, from a trader pursuing an unpaid debt to a family contesting land ownership. When cases drag on, businesses lose money, relationships deteriorate and confidence in lawful solutions weakens. Independence needs resources “Even judges must eat” captures an important truth. Judges and court workers need decent conditions, while courts need buildings, records, equipment and functioning systems. Independence requires the means to do the work. Ghana’s Constitution already recognises this. Article 127 protects judicial independence, including financial administration. It charges judicial administrative expenses on the Consolidated Fund, protects conditions of service and requires quarterly releases of judicial funds. The Judicial Service Act, 2020, also provides for administration, funding, audit and reporting. The challenge is making these protections work. Citizens should be able to see what courts request, what Parliament approves, what is released and how the money is spent. Institutions receiving public funds must explain both their needs and their results. A 1988 study published by the Centre for the Independence of Judges and Lawyers makes a distinction that remains useful: freedom to decide cases must be supported by security in employment and material conditions. Constitutional promises lose value when inflation erodes salaries or funding commitments go unmet. Appointments must inspire confidence Under Article 144, Supreme Court appointments involve the President, Judicial Council, Council of State and Parliament. Sharing responsibility creates safeguards, but procedures must also inspire public confidence. In Ghana Bar Association and Others v Attorney-General and Others, decided in 2016, the Supreme Court confirmed that a Supreme Court appointment requires a Judicial Council recommendation, although the President need not appoint every recommended person. The Constitution Review Committee proposes more structured selection procedures. Government’s July 2026 Position Paper rejects the proposed constitutional changes to appointment processes, favouring existing arrangements. These differences deserve public debate. Published vacancies, clear criteria and transparent procedures would help citizens judge whether merit drives appointments. Britain’s Constitutional Reform Act 2005 established a Judicial Appointments Commission, operating from 2006 principally in England and Wales. Ghana need not copy it, but can learn from its emphasis on merit and good character. Protection must reach Circuit and District Courts too. Existing constitutional safeguards should be acknowledged, while staffing, working conditions and disciplinary procedures receive serious attention. Most citizens experience justice through these courts. Social pressure matters Political interference is only part of the problem. Public officials also face demands from relatives, friends, schoolmates, religious communities and party supporters. Requests for preferential treatment often arrive as appeals to loyalty or gratitude. My 2008 doctoral research at Oxford Brookes University examined cultural and institutional pressures through surveys and 35 interviews. Discussing approaches to judges on behalf of relatives, participant PA2 argued: “He should be cut off from such things so that when he goes he reads the case and gives objective judgements.” This illustrates perceived pressure from personal connections; it does not establish that all judges yield to it. Family solidarity is valuable. So are funerals, weddings and community celebrations. However, expectations of lavish spending and reciprocal favours can place pressure on public workers. Better salaries help, but cannot replace ethical boundaries. Articles 284 and 286 already address conflicts of interest and asset declarations. Enforcement matters. Public office should never become a means of financing social status or rewarding personal networks. Respect for authority should allow questioning. Community loyalty should coexist with impartiality. Our cultural strengths include investment in children’s education and mutual support; reform should build on these while challenging practices that undermine fairness. Technology should improve justice Digital reform deserves sustained investment. Electronic filing, searchable records, digital payments and reliable hearing schedules could reduce missing files, unnecessary journeys and opportunities for unofficial payments. Case management systems should record adjournments and their reasons, helping judges identify avoidable delays. Appropriate remote hearings could save time without weakening fair participation. Citizens should be able to track cases and obtain published judgments. Public reporting should show case age, vacancies, expenditure and performance. However, judges should not be pressured to sacrifice careful decisions merely to improve disposal figures. Technology also needs maintenance, training, cybersecurity and proper judicial control. People without internet access or digital skills must receive assistance. A computer system that excludes citizens cannot deliver accessible justice. Reform must also address political financing. When financial support for parties is treated as an investment to be repaid through appointments, contracts or access, public institutions become vulnerable to private interests. Transparent financing and credible scrutiny can help interrupt that cycle. A shared national responsibility Afrobarometer’s 2024 survey found that only 35% of Ghanaians trusted courts somewhat or a lot, compared with 57% in 2017. Such perceptions underline the need to rebuild confidence through visible fairness and accountability. Citizens, journalists and professional bodies have responsibilities too. They should scrutinise decisions, demand reliable information and challenge wrongdoing without assuming every unpopular judgment reflects corruption. Protecting legitimate authority and questioning its use are compatible democratic duties. The CRC’s recommendations emerged from nationwide consultation. Government’s position is an executive response, not the end of the conversation. Where proposals differ, citizens deserve clear explanations and genuine efforts to find agreement. Ghana needs transparent appointments, predictable funding, stronger oversight, effective ethical enforcement and technology that improves services. Some changes require constitutional amendment; others require legislation or implementation of safeguards already in place. It behoves all well-meaning Ghanaians to help secure agreement on necessary reforms and hold authorities accountable for delivery. Constitutional reform must become a shared national responsibility that survives changes of government. Institutions should belong to the Republic. Their authority must serve all citizens fairly, their resources must match their responsibilities, and their independence must be accompanied by accountability.

items.title: Military arrests two over attack on vigilantes, burning of Jos office
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa Troops of Operation Enduring Peace, OPEP, have arrested two suspects over an alleged attack on members of a vigilante group and the subsequent burning of their office in Jos North Local Government Area of Plateau State. The suspects were arrested at about 1:40 a.m. on October 27, 2026, in the NEPA area of Jos North. Media Information Officer of OPEP, Capt. Chinonso Polycarp Oteh, who confirmed the arrests, said the suspects were apprehended by troops of Sector 1, OPEP. Oteh said, “The arrest followed allegations linking the suspects to the attack on vigilante personnel and the subsequent setting ablaze of their office.” He said, “The suspects are currently in custody for further investigation and necessary action.” Oteh said, “The arrests form part of ongoing efforts by OPEP to tackle criminal activities and maintain peace across Plateau State.” He added, “Security personnel will continue to intensify operations aimed at identifying and apprehending individuals involved in acts capable of undermining peace and security in the state.” ” We call on members of the public to cooperate with the military and other security agencies by providing timely and credible information that could assist in preventing criminal activities and apprehending suspects.” Oteh said, “The continued cooperation and support of members of the public remain crucial to our efforts to maintain peace and security across the state.” He added, “Security personnel will continue to intensify operations aimed at identifying and apprehending individuals involved in acts capable of undermining peace and security in the state.” The post Military arrests two over attack on vigilantes, burning of Jos office appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Algérie Ferries : le Tariq Ibn Ziyad immobilisé à Alicante
items.description: Le Tariq Ibn Ziyad, navire emblématique de la compagnie algérienne de transport de voyageurs Algérie Ferries , est de nouveau bloqué dans un port étranger. Le ferry algérien est immobilisé depuis mardi 27 octobre au port espagnol d’Alicante, rapporte mardi le média français spécialisé dans la navigation maritime, Le Marin. Le Tariq Ibn Ziyad retenu à Alicante pour des “déficiences” Le Tariq Ibn Ziyad est retenu pour “des déficiences dans le cadre du contrôle de l’État du port du Mémorandum de Paris”, indique la même source, ajoutant que la nature des déficiences “n’est pas connue à ce stade”. Le navire a repris la navigation au printemps dernier après une immobilisation de plus de deux ans, entre février 2024 et mars 2026, au chantier grec Onex d’Eleusis suite à un accident survenu à Alicante à l’été 2023, rappelle Le Marin. Le Badji Mokhtar 3 est sur un chantier grec depuis mai dernier Le journal signale qu’un autre des quatre navires d’Algérie Ferries, le Badji Mokhtar 3, est aussi hors service depuis mai dernier. Il se trouve toujours immobilisé au même chantier grec. Le Badji Mokhtar 3 a quitté le service juste avant la pleine saison alors que, souligne le média, “ce genre d’opération est programmée en basse saison”. La compagnie algérienne avait expliqué qu’il s’agissait d’un “arrêt technique prévu de longue date”. “La raison pour laquelle son indisponibilité dure n’est pas claire”, écrit Le Marin, qui signale en outre qu'un autre navire d’Algérie ferries, El Djazaïr 2, “n’a pas quitté l’Algérie depuis début octobre.” L’article Algérie Ferries : le Tariq Ibn Ziyad immobilisé à Alicante est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Ecobank maintient sa dynamique de croissance sur les neufs premiers mois de 2026, avec un produit net bancaire de 2 milliards USD et un bénéfice avant impôt de 737 millions USD
items.description: Points clés Le produit net bancaire (PNB) progresse de 12 % en glissement annuel, à 2 milliards USD, tandis que le résultat avant impôt augmente de 12 %, à 737 millions USD, témoignant de la solidité des performances du Groupe malgré un environnement macroéconomique et géopolitique difficile. L'efficacité opérationnelle poursuit son amélioration, avec un coefficient d'exploitation ramené à 47,8 %, soit une performance supérieure à l'objectif fixé par le Groupe pour 2026. Les dépôts de la clientèle progressent de 14% en glissement annuel, pour atteindre 27,5 milliards USD, confirmant la confiance des clients et la solidité de la base de dépôts d'Ecobank. Les performances demeurent diversifiées, tant sur le plan géographique que par ligne de métier. Le résultat avant impôt progresse de 20 % en Afrique centrale, orientale et australe (CESA) et de 10 % en Afrique de l'Ouest anglophone (AWA), soutenu par les contributions des activités de Banque de Grande Clientèle et d'Investissement (CIB) et de Banque Commerciale et de Détail (CCB). Lomé, Togo, 27 octobre 2026 – Le groupe Ecobank annonce la poursuite de sa croissance au cours des neuf premiers mois de 2026, dans un environnement marqué par des tensions inflationnistes, la volatilité des taux de change et un ralentissement de l'activité économique dans certains marchés africains. Sur la période, le Groupe enregistre un bénéfice avant impôt de 737 millions USD, en hausse de 12 % par rapport à la même période en 2025, tandis que le produit net bancaire atteint 2 milliards USD, soit une progression de 12 %. Ces performances reposent notamment sur la poursuite des efforts d'optimisation opérationnelle, la mobilisation des dépôts de la clientèle, les investissements technologiques et la mise en œuvre rigoureuse de la stratégie « Croissance, Transformation et Rendements » (GTR) du Groupe. Ecobank poursuit également le renforcement de son bilan, avec des dépôts de la clientèle atteignant 27,5 milliards USD, tout en maintenant une position solide en matière de liquidité et de fonds propres. Le coefficient d'exploitation s'établit à 47,8 %, dépassant ainsi l'objectif de performance fixé pour 2026, compris entre 48 % et 50 %. Cette évolution traduit les résultats des initiatives engagées pour améliorer durablement l'efficacité opérationnelle dans l'ensemble du Groupe. La diversification géographique et la complémentarité des métiers d'Ecobank ont également contribué à la résilience de ses résultats. En Afrique centrale, orientale et australe (CESA), le résultat avant impôt progresse de 20 %, tandis que l'Afrique de l'Ouest anglophone (AWA) affiche une croissance de 10 %, compensant les performances plus modérées enregistrées en Afrique de l'Ouest francophone (UEMOA) et au Nigeria. Cette dynamique illustre la capacité du modèle panafricain du Groupe à absorber les disparités de performance entre ses différents marchés. Les activités de la Banque des Grandes Entreprises et d'Investissement (CIB) et de la Banque Commerciale et des Particuliers (CCB) continuent, par ailleurs, de contribuer de manière équilibrée aux résultats du Groupe. Les paiements et les services bancaires numériques demeurent des leviers essentiels de croissance. Les revenus issus des activités de paiement progressent de 9 %, portés par les investissements continus dans les infrastructures technologiques et les plateformes digitales, avec pour objectif d'améliorer l'expérience client et d'accélérer l'inclusion financière sur le continent. Déclaration du Directeur général du Groupe Commentant ces résultats, Jeremy Awori, directeur général du Groupe Ecobank , a déclaré : « Nous avons réalisé un bénéfice avant impôt de 737 millions USD, en progression de 12 % sur un an, et enregistré une rentabilité des fonds propres tangibles de 24,9 %. Notre produit net bancaire a également augmenté de 12 %, pour atteindre 2 milliards USD. » Il a poursuivi : « Les résultats obtenus en matière d'efficacité opérationnelle et de développement de notre portefeuille clientèle témoignent de la pertinence de notre stratégie Croissance, Transformation et Rendements (GTR). Notre coefficient d'exploitation s'établit à 47,8 %, soit un niveau plus favorable que notre objectif 2026, fixé entre 48 % et 50 %. Les dépôts de la clientèle ont progressé de 14 %, pour atteindre 27,5 milliards USD, dont 85 % sont constitués de dépôts à vue et de comptes d'épargne. Cette évolution reflète la confiance que nous accordent nos clients, qui choisissent Ecobank pour leurs opérations bancaires quotidiennes. Cette croissance des dépôts nous a permis d'atténuer les pressions exercées sur les marges par le cycle de baisse des taux d'intérêt observé sur nos marchés, tout en soutenant une progression de 12 % de nos revenus nets d'intérêts. Les revenus des activités de paiement ont également augmenté de 9 %, grâce à nos investissements continus dans la technologie et les plateformes digitales. La solidité de notre modèle économique diversifié s'illustre également dans les performances régionales, avec une hausse du résultat avant impôt de 20 % en Afrique centrale, orientale et australe (CESA) et de 10 % en Afrique de l'Ouest anglophone (AWA), permettant de compenser les résultats plus modérés enregistrés en Afrique de l'Ouest francophone (UEMOA) et au Nigeria. » Jeremy Awori a également souligné : « Notre taux de créances douteuses (NPL) est resté globalement stable au cours du trimestre, à 7,5 %, conformément à notre fourchette cible de 6 % à 8 % pour 2026. Cette stabilité traduit la rigueur de notre gestion du portefeuille de crédits et notre discipline en matière de gestion des risques. » En conclusion, il a indiqué : « L'évolution des prix de l'énergie, les tensions inflationnistes et la volatilité des taux de change demeurent des facteurs de risque pour les prochains mois. Toutefois, la solidité de notre base de dépôts, notre position de liquidité et notre assise en fonds propres, associées au développement de nouvelles offres et solutions pour nos clients, nous donnent les moyens de poursuivre notre croissance tout en maintenant une gestion prudente des risques. Nous restons sur la bonne voie pour atteindre nos objectifs pour 2026. Je tiens à remercier l'ensemble des collaborateurs d'Ecobank pour leur engagement et leur mobilisation quotidienne au service de nos clients. » Une dynamique qui va au-delà des résultats financiers Au cours du trimestre, Ecobank a poursuivi le renforcement de son positionnement international, notamment à travers l'inauguration de ses nouveaux locaux de représentation à Pékin et la signature d'un protocole d'accord avec le système interbancaire chinois de paiements transfrontaliers (CIPS). Ces initiatives marquent une nouvelle étape dans le développement des échanges commerciaux et financiers entre la Chine et l'Afrique. Le Groupe a également clôturé les célébrations de son 40e anniversaire en annonçant un engagement de 2,6 milliards USD destiné à soutenir les entreprises détenues ou dirigées par des femmes ainsi que le développement du secteur agricole à travers l'Afrique. Le leadership d'Ecobank a, par ailleurs, été salué lors des Global Finance Awards, organisés en marge des Assemblées annuelles de la Banque mondiale et du Fonds monétaire international (FMI). Le Groupe s'est notamment vu décerner les distinctions de « Meilleure banque en Afrique 2026 » et de « Meilleure banque mondiale sur les marchés frontières 2026 ». Ces distinctions viennent conforter l'engagement d'Ecobank en faveur de l'innovation, de l'excellence du service client et d'une croissance durable au bénéfice des économies africaines. Le Groupe emploie plus de 14 000 personnes et propose des produits, services et solutions de banque de détail, banque commerciale, banque de grande entreprise et banque d’investissement à plus de 30 millions de clients, à travers de multiples canaux, y compris numériques. items.description: En séjour à Moscou dans le cadre du troisième Sommet Russie–Afrique, le Camarade Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a accordé, le 27 octobre 2026, un entretien exclusif au média RT (Russia Today). Conduit par le journaliste Igor Kurashenko, cet entretien a principalement porté sur la lutte contre l’impérialisme, la maîtrise des ressources nationales et la construction de partenariats respectueux de la souveraineté du Burkina Faso. Lors de cet entretien d'une trentaine de minutes, le Chef du Gouvernement a réaffirmé la détermination du Burkina Faso à décider librement de son avenir. Dénonçant les rapports de domination, les accords déséquilibrés et les ingérences, il a rappelé que la rupture avec la politique impérialiste française répondait à une exigence d’émancipation. « Nous n’avons rien contre le peuple français », a-t-il précisé, tout en défendant le droit du peuple burkinabè à être maître de son destin. « Nous avons quitté un type de coopération pour un autre type de coopération. » Par cette déclaration, le Premier ministre a répondu aux discours assimilant le rapprochement avec Moscou à un changement de tutelle. Il a mis en avant une coopération honnête, transparente, d’égal à égal et fondée sur les intérêts des deux peuples. Les attentes du Burkina Faso à ce sommet ont traduit cette ambition en objectifs concrets : renforcer la formation, les transferts de technologies et les capacités nationales de production. Produire suffisamment pour se nourrir, transformer les ressources minières sur place et développer les compétences nationales : telles sont les priorités défendues par le Chef du Gouvernement, dans la mise en œuvre de la vision du Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré. La reconquête du territoire a également occupé une place importante dans l’entretien. Le Premier ministre a fait état d’une amélioration significative et continue de la situation sécuritaire. Il a précisé que le chiffre de plus de 74 % du territoire consolidé concernait les zones reconquises, sécurisées durablement et où les populations déplacées avaient pu se réinstaller. Il a aussi souligné l’apport du partenariat russe à la prise en main des équipements et au renforcement des capacités des Forces combattantes. Cette lutte pour la souveraineté, portée avec le Mali et le Niger au sein de la Confédération des États du Sahel, comporte également une dimension informationnelle. Le Chef du Gouvernement a dénoncé les campagnes de désinformation visant les États de l'AES et plaidé pour des relations internationales fondées sur le respect des peuples. À travers cet entretien, le Premier ministre a porté l'orientation claire de la Révolution progressiste populaire, notamment dans son volet diplomatique : bâtir des partenariats qui renforcent les capacités du Burkina Faso, préservent sa liberté de choix et servent les aspirations de son peuple. items.title: Terres rares : une mission conjointe Cameroun-USA à Minta
items.description: © DR Le 27 octobre 2026, le ministre des Mines Fuh Calistus Gentry, s’est rendu à Minta à la Haute-Sanaga, avec une délégation de l’ambassade des États-Unis. Objectif : suivre le projet d’exploration des terres rares de Lion Rock Minerals et ses retombées pour le Cameroun. Minta devient un symbole de la nouvelle diplomatie minière du Cameroun. Le 27 octobre 2026, le ministre des Mines, de l’Industrie et du Développement Technologique, Fuh Calistus Gentry, y a effectué une visite de terrain, accompagné d’une délégation de l’ambassade des États-Unis, conduite par le Chargé d’Affaires. La descente s’inscrit dans le suivi du projet d’exploration des terres rares et d’autres minerais stratégiques mené par Lion Rock Minerals, en partenariat avec l’entreprise américaine Tronox. Accueillie par les autorités administratives, municipales et traditionnelles, la délégation a fait le point sur l’avancement du projet et ses perspectives. Parmi les retombées annoncées : l’extension envisagée du réseau ferroviaire sur environ 40 km jusqu’au site minier, le renforcement de l’approvisionnement énergétique et la création d’emplois pour les populations locales. Dans son allocution, le ministre a salué les investissements de Lion Rock Minerals et l’accompagnement du gouvernement américain. Il a réaffirmé l’engagement du Cameroun pour un développement minier responsable, générateur d’emplois, favorisant le transfert de technologies et la valorisation locale des ressources. La visite s’est poursuivie sur le site de Nguen, où les activités d’exploration ont été présentées. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans la vision de faire du secteur minier un levier majeur de l’industrialisation et du développement économique du Cameroun. Cet article Terres rares : une mission conjointe Cameroun-USA à Minta est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: 'Conscience does not permit': LHC's Justice Kayani resigns, cites 'executive's growing control' over judiciary
items.description: LAHORE: Lahore High Court’s (LHC) Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani resigned on Wednesday, citing personal reasons, including health concerns following a recent surgery, and “reasons of conscience”. In his resignation letter to the president of Pakistan, a copy of which is available with Dawn , Justice Kayani said it had been a privilege for him to serve at the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and LHC. “These years of judicial service remain among the most meaningful and fulfilling of my life. During my tenure, I have disposed of more than 23,000 cases of various categories, endeavouring always to uphold the Constitution, safeguard fundamental rights, and administer justice without fear or favour,” he continued. However, he added, “in my considered view, the changes introduced through the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments have compromised the independence and institutional integrity of the high courts”. “I have witnessed what I regard as the executive’s growing control over judicial institutions, extending to the appointment and transfer of judges. Such interference has, in my assessment, seriously eroded public confidence in judicial independence and the fairness of the judicial process.” Justice Kayani stated that of particular concern was the plight of the ordinary litigant, “who is the principal stakeholder in the justice system, yet whose suffering continues to deepen”. The needs of those seeking justice had too often been neglected, while other actors had become the “beneficiaries of a system intended to serve them”, he said. “In these circumstances, my conscience does not permit me to continue on the bench. This is a painful decision, but it reflects my conviction that judicial office must remain inseparable from independence, fidelity to the Constitution, and the protection of human dignity. “I, therefore, consider that the time has come for me to lay down my robes and return to legal practice, through which I intend to continue serving the people, protecting their rights, and promoting legal awareness,” he added. The judge ended his letter expressing gratitude to “my teachers, fellow judges and family members for their guidance and steadfast support, including during the deliberations that led to this decision”. His resignation has come years before the date of his retirement — Feb 10, 2032. He hails from Islamabad and was serving at the IHC before his transfer to the LHC in April. He was assigned to the LHC’s principal seat in Lahore. Despite being a senior judge of the LHC, he was not assigned to any division bench. Justice Kayani previously served as the senior puisne judge of the IHC and was expecting to be elevated to the post of the high court’s chief justice. However, the transfer of incumbent IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar from the LHC, along with two other judges from the Sindh and Balochistan high courts, prompted him to challenge the inter-high court transfers. The Supreme Court’s constitutional bench upheld the transfers to the IHC, including that of Justice Dogar. The decision, however, triggered a broader legal battle. Justice Kayani and other senior IHC judges approached the Supreme Court to challenge the administrative powers exercised by Chief Justice Dogar. They alleged that the office had been turned into a “monocracy” and that judges could be excluded from the roster at will. Following his own transfer to the LHC, Justice Kayani lost his seniority and was placed 12th on the high court’s seniority list. His resignation came days after he returned to the twin cities to preside over a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry following a reshuffle at the high court. The new duty roster assigned him only to a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry despite his previous position as the IHC’s senior puisne judge. Justice Kayani was also one of the six IHC judges who had accused the country’s intelligence apparatus of interference in judicial affairs, including attempts to pressure judges through abduction and torture of their relatives and secret surveillance inside their homes in a startling letter to the Supreme Judicial Council (SJC) members in March 2024. Education and career According to information available on the LHC’s website, Justice Kayani completed his early education at FG Boys High School in Islamabad and pursued higher education at FG College for Men. He graduated in 1989. The judge earned his LLB from the University of Punjab in 1994, followed by an MA degree in Political Science in 1996, an LLM from Karachi University in 2003 and a MSc in Pakistan Studies in 2005. He also has postgraduate diploma in human rights from Peshawar University in collaboration with the Norwegian Institute of Human Rights, Oslo University. Justice Kayani was enrolled as an advocate of the district courts in 1995 and ascended to the high court in 1997 and the Supreme Court in 2009. He was appointed as an IHC judge on Dec 23, 2015 and transferred to the LHC on April 29 this year. The judge also served as the joint secretary of the Islamabad District Bar Association from 1998 to 1999, general secretary of the Islamabad District Bar Association from 2002 to 2003 and the president of the Islamabad High Court Bar Association from 2013 to 2014. “He has presided over significant cases, particularly those related to enforced disappearances. Justice Kayani has advocated for legislative reforms, including proposing strict penalties for enforced disappearances, reflecting his commitment to justice and the rule of law,” the website says.

items.title: Inscriptions ouvertes pour le 39e Marathon Comar de Tunis-Carthage
items.description: Les inscriptions pour la participation à la 39 e édition du Marathon Comar de Tunis-Carthage , qui aura lieu le dimanche 6 décembre 2026, sont ouvertes. Créé en 1986 par les Assurances Comar, ce rendez-vous à la fois sportif, culturel, touristique et écologique s’est imposé comme un rendez-vous populaire annuel très attendu. Il draine chaque année près de 8 000 athlètes, amateurs et professionnels, tunisiens et étrangers, qui viennent participer aux quatre courses programmées : le Marathon, le semi-Marathon, la course pour tous et le Kids Marathon. Enregistré sur le calendrier national tunisien géré par la Fédération tunisienne d’athlétisme (FTA) et aussi, depuis 2019, sur le calendrier international de la Fédération internationale d’athlétisme géré par World Athletics, le Marathon Comar est devenu, au fil des ans, le plus grand événement sportif outdoor en Tunisie et l’événement phare incontournable dans l’histoire de la course à pied dans le pays. Fort de son héritage et de son leadership, il est considéré comme le plus ancien et le plus important marathon organisé en Afrique du Nord. Certifié par l’Association des marathons internationaux (AIMS), il est ouvert à toutes les catégories (professionnels et amateurs, hommes et femmes, enfants et séniors) et à tous les paysdu Maghreb, d’Europe et au-delà, il œuvre à encourager l’activité physique régulière à travers la course à pied et à préserver la santé et le bien-être de coureurs. Les athlètes en quête de performances y prennent part et sont de plus en plus nombreux chaque année à s’aligner sur sa ligne de départ, ainsi que les coureurs de dimanche qui cherchent çà entretenir leur forme physique, sans oublier les simples spectateurs qui viennent prendre part à une fête populaire au cœur de la capitale et sa banlieue. Depuis la 34ᵉ édition en 2019, le Marathon Comar œuvre à honorer son engagement environnemental pour la protection de la planète grâce au reboisement des espaces forestiers détruits par les incendies des arbres, le but étant d’atteindre, à moyen terme, l’objectif d’un événement avec zéro empreinte carbone. Des opérations de reboisement sont ainsi organisées, régulièrement, en partenariat avec l’association Tounes Clean Up, par la plantation de centaines de milliers d’arbres à travers la Tunisie. Lien pour s’inscrire aux quatre courses programmées : Marathon (42,195 KM), Semi Marathon (21,1 KM), Course pour tous (5 KM) et Course Kids (1,2 KM). I. B. L’article Inscriptions ouvertes pour le 39e Marathon Comar de Tunis-Carthage est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47bn, according to Pentagon estimate
items.description: The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran , more than 25 per cent higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters . The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly. The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict. More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “ platform losses ,” which include the loss of aircraft, including many drones lost during the war. Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time. Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful. But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible. Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so. The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war. While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

items.title: Cameroun : le marché historique de Mora démoli, Mamadou Mota interpelle le préfet du Mayo-Sava
items.description: © DR La démolition du marché de Mora cette nuit suscite la colère de Mamadou Mota, élite de la localité et ancien vice-président du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun. Il demande au préfet de prendre ses responsabilités en main. Il ne reste plus que des décombres de ce qui était jusqu’à mardi soir des boutiques et comptoirs du marché de Mora. Des installations de l’espace marchand ont disparu de la place cette nuit. D’après des témoins, la mairie de la commune de Mora a procédé aux environs de 3h du matin à leur démolition. Un acte qui complète le processus de déguerpissement de la place occupée par le marché historique de la permanence. Ce que Mamadou Mota digère mal. D’après l’élite de la localité comme il se présente lui-même, « c’est un acte d’une lâcheté absolue ». Les populations sont déjà fragilisées par l’insécurité galopante dans le Mayo-Sava. Le maire vient encore « anéantir leurs maigres moyens de subsistance ». Il qualifie cette démolition de « trahison intolérable » et déclare que « les coupables de ce désastre économique et social doivent payer ». Dans sa sortie il interpelle le préfet autorité de tutelle de la commune en lui demandant de prendre ses responsabilités. Sur la place du marché, le processus de déguerpissement a été entrepris il des mois par la mairie qui a initié et met en œuvre le projet de construction du marché moderne de Sankré. Première phase du projet achevé, le maire a lancé le transfert des activités commerciales de l’ancien marché vers le marché moderne. Mais, les populations et commerçants ont manifesté leur résistance. En mars dernier, le maire Chetima Hamidou parti pour détruire des boutiques au marché historique a été encerclé par des populations qui ont opposé une vive résistance à la démolition, prétextant que le nouveau marché ne contient pas assez de boutiques pour recaser tout le monde. Plus tard, la réalité a commencé à changer. Sur environ 87 commerçants et artisans recensés sur la place de l’ancien marché, plus de la moitié avaient rejoint le nouveau marché. Le maire a lancé la deuxième phase du projet avec dans le viseur la construction de 180 boutiques, trois hangars, une boucherie, deux blocs sanitaires et une mosquée. Le 28 septembre, le premier magistrat municipal signait encore des arrêtés portant transfert de certaines activités du marché historique vers le marché moderne. Ce mercredi matin, la démolition du marché historique est une réalité. Ce même mercredi, la permanence du parti RDPC de Mora a été ravagé par des flammes. Certains lient cet incendie à la démolition du marché, pointant un doigt accusateur sur certains habitants qui auraient agi en représailles contre les autorités municipales. Cet article Cameroun : le marché historique de Mora démoli, Mamadou Mota interpelle le préfet du Mayo-Sava est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Muslims in Texas seek greater political influence ahead of US midterm elections
items.description: WASHINGTON: Mosques in Houston are doubling as voter registration centres ahead of the Nov 3 midterms , and local Muslim leaders say they are helping sign up around 1,000 voters a week. The drive in Texas’s metropolis follows the Republican-majority State Board of Education’s approval of a new social studies curriculum that Muslim advocates say portrays Islam unfairly. The contentious high school curriculum, for instance, requires students to learn that “radical Islam” motivated the 9/11 attacks instead of focusing on the terrorist groups involved. But supporters of the new curriculum defend it as part of a broader emphasis on Western civilisation and the foundations of the United States and Texas. The dispute has become one example of a broader question facing Muslim Americans: can greater political organisation help them influence public policy and counter discrimination? In the American political system, advocacy caucuses play a key role in influencing public policy and elections by mobilising voters around shared concerns. They register voters, educate communities, support candidates and lobby elected officials. Groups such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) illustrate how organised advocacy can shape political debate. For Muslim Americans, similar groups offer a way to pool electoral influence, engage candidates and press for attention to their concerns, particularly in closely contested races. Their concerns range from civil rights, immigration and the economy to US foreign policy, particularly its approach to the Middle East. Yet a growing political presence does not necessarily translate into electoral power, nor are Muslim Americans a unified voting bloc: their party affiliations, social views and policy priorities vary considerably. On November 3, Texas voters will decide several key federal and state races, including a closely watched US Senate contest, the governorship and all 38 seats in the US House of Representatives. Republican Ken Paxton, Democrat James Talarico and Libertarian Ted Brown are contesting the Senate seat, while Republican Governor Greg Abbott is seeking a fourth term against Democratic nominee Gina Hinojosa and Libertarian Pat Dixon. All 150 seats in the Texas House of Representatives and 16 of the state Senate’s 31 seats are also up for election, alongside other statewide offices, State Board of Education seats, judgeships and local positions. Syed Hassan, the co-chair of the American Muslim Democratic Caucus, stresses the need for political organisation against this backdrop. Speaking at the caucus’s 2026 national convention, he recalled former US president Barack Obama telling the 2004 Democratic National Convention in Boston that “there is no Black America and White America, no liberal America and conservative America — only the United States of America”. A small gathering of Muslim delegates at a mosque in Cambridge around that time helped inspire the caucus, he said. Hassan urged underrepresented communities to organise around shared democratic concerns. “Our strategy is simple: we unite, we organise, we vote,” he said. He warned that hostility directed at one minority could eventually shift to another. “Last election, it was our hardworking, honest Mexican and Latino brothers and sisters in the crosshairs. This time, it is hatred against Muslims. Next time, it will be another community entirely,” he said. Hassan’s approach reflects one strand of Muslim political activism: using elections and party organisations to defend civil rights and influence decisions affecting the community. Others, including Muslim Republicans and independents, pursue a different approach. Sajid Tarar, a Pakistani-American businessman and founder of American Muslims for Trump, is urging Muslims to support Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. A strong ally of President Donald Trump, Tarar argues that “the Republican platform best serves the interests, safety, and economic prosperity of the Muslim community in the United States.” A growing community, a divided electorate The Pew Research Centre estimated in September that the United States now has about 5.5 million Muslims of all ages, up from 2.4 million in 2007. The figure can be seen as an indication of a growing religious and institutional presence of Muslims, but population growth alone does not establish how many Muslims are eligible to vote, registered or likely to turn out. Muslims account for a relatively small share of the national electorate, although their concentration in particular cities and electoral districts can make their participation significant in some local and closely contested races. Survey data about their political affiliations also challenge the assumption that Muslim voters overwhelmingly favour Democrats. Pew’s analysis of its 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study — in which 1.2 per cent of 36,908 respondents in the US identified as Muslims — found that 53pc of Muslim adults identified with or leaned towards the Democratic Party while 42pc identified with or leaned towards the Republican Party. On immigration and the value of racial and ethnic diversity, Muslim Americans tended to hold views closer to those of Democrats. On some questions involving family, sexuality and gender identity, their views were closer to those of Republicans. Other issues divided opinion within the community. Such differences complicate efforts to build a common political agenda. Religious identity may encourage collective action on certain issues, but it does not determine how individual Muslims vote. Texas becomes a political battleground Texas offers an example of how disputes over education, religious freedom and the public perception of Islam are spurring political engagement. In Houston, the Islamic Society of Greater Houston has sought to bring more Muslims into the electoral process. Its president, Emran Gazi, said at a press conference last month that the organisation was helping register about 1,000 voters a week at mosques across the city. Apart from the curriculum revision, controversies have centred on campaigns against what some Republican politicians describe as the threat of Sharia law to Western values and the US Constitution. Texas Republican state representative Brent Money established the Sharia-Free Texas Caucus while US representatives Keith Self and Chip Roy helped launch a Sharia-Free America Caucus in Congress. Texas Governor Abbott has also challenged Muslim ablution facilities at two major airports, arguing that they raised legal questions about religious accommodation. In a letter to the Department of Justice in August, he sought a federal probe into the airport ‌facilities, a move that a Muslim advocacy group called an “anti-Muslim political stunt”. These disputes have added urgency for voter registration and advocacy efforts among some Muslim Texans. But the state’s political dynamics cannot be taken as representative of the entire country. Muslim communities in Michigan, New York, Illinois, New Jersey, Minnesota and Virginia operate in different electoral environments, and Muslims have won office at both state and national levels. Foreign policy and party loyalty US policy in the Middle East, particularly the Israeli assault in Gaza , has become another important factor in Muslim political organising. For some voters, foreign policy is a measure of whether candidates and parties take their concerns seriously. Others place greater weight on the economy, healthcare, immigration, civil liberties or social issues. These competing priorities make it difficult to assess Muslim political influence solely through party affiliation. A voter may support one party on domestic issues while opposing its foreign policy. Another may hold conservative social views but object to anti-Muslim rhetoric or restrictive immigration measures. For Hassan, the challenge is to turn political participation into a more effective voice in public affairs. “We, the people, are the special interest now. Not them,” Hassan told his caucus’s convention, criticising the influence of wealthy donors and lobbyists and calling for a more equal political system. Whether that ambition translates into measurable influence will depend on more than voter-registration drives. Turnout, geographic concentration, coalition-building and the willingness of candidates and elected officials to respond to Muslim Americans’ concerns will all help determine how much political weight the community can exercise. Header image: Young Muslims protest then-US Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump before being escorted out during a campaign rally in Wichita, Kansas, March 5, 2016. — Reuters/ File

items.title: CEMAC : 251 tonnes de faux médicaments saisies
items.description: © DR À la 13ᵉ Conférence des Nations Unies contre la criminalité transfrontalière, la CEMAC a présenté à Vienne un rapport de l’ONUDC et de l’OMS. Le constat est alarmant : entre 2020 et 2025, plus de 251 tonnes de produits médicaux ont été saisies en Afrique centrale et 71 % des échantillons analysés sont falsifiés. Le trafic de faux médicaments est devenu une menace sanitaire et sécuritaire majeure en Afrique centrale. C’est le message porté la semaine dernière à Vienne, en Autriche, par la délégation de la Commission de la CEMAC, conduite par le Commissaire en charge du Marché commun, Mbogo Ngabo Seli. Accompagné de M. Algadi Atim Oumar, directeur de la criminalité transnationale au CCPAC, et de M. Abdon Fortuné Ngoma, chef de service de la libre circulation, il a pris part à la 13ᵉ Conférence des Nations Unies contre la criminalité transfrontalière. À cette occasion a été officiellement présenté le rapport intitulé « Le trafic de produits médicaux en Afrique centrale », un document inédit de l’ONUDC et de l’OMS, en partenariat avec la Commission de la CEMAC. Les chiffres sont vertigineux. Entre 2020 et 2025, plus de 251 tonnes de produits médicaux ont été saisies dans la zone. Plus grave encore : 71 % des échantillons analysés par l’OMS se sont révélés être des produits falsifiés. Ces réseaux criminels ne se contentent pas de tromper les patients. Ils infiltrent les circuits réglementés, mettent en danger des millions de vies et financent des groupes armés, menaçant la stabilité sanitaire et sécuritaire de la région. Face à ce fléau aux conséquences mortelles, la CEMAC en appelle à une coopération internationale renforcée. La Commission a dévoilé une feuille de route régionale 2026-2030, axée sur le renseignement, l’harmonisation des législations et le contrôle strict des grands corridors commerciaux. À Vienne, l’Afrique centrale a parlé d’une seule voix : la lutte contre les faux médicaments n’est plus seulement une question de santé, c’est un impératif de sécurité collective. Cet article CEMAC : 251 tonnes de faux médicaments saisies est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
